thread.title_full: Lessenberry: Trump finally endorses in Michigan gubernatorial race - NewsBreak

author: JACK LESSENBERRY
title: Lessenberry: Trump finally endorses in Michigan gubernatorial race - NewsBreak
text:
By JACK LESSENBERRY ,
1 hours ago
DETROIT — Michigan, for the first time in the state’s long history, has both an open governor and an open U.S. Senate race on the ballot this year. The senate contest has drawn vast attention, but the governor’s race less so, especially in the last month.
That may seem baffling, and no politician will say why this is, at least not on the record. But what’s really happening is this:
Republicans think they have little chance to win the governor’s race, especially since former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan stunned the state by ending his independent bid. Meanwhile, keeping control of the U.S. Senate is the party’s top priority.
There’s near-total consensus that while Democrats may not win the majority even if they hold on to the seat now held by the retiring Gary Peters, they have no hope of doing so if they lose it.
Looked at one way, the GOP should be favored in the governor’s race, too. Since 1960, every time an incumbent governor has retired, she or he has been replaced by a governor of the party that was out of office. Term limits mean that Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer has to leave forever at the end of this year.
But the party that controls the White House normally does poorly in midterm elections, and all signs indicate a bigger-than-normal backlash this year against Republicans, both nationally and in Michigan. It is also still not clear who the GOP candidate will be.
U.S. Rep. John James, one of the few African-American Republican office holders, was seen as a phenomenon and the party’s future five years ago. A businessman with a distinguished war record as an Army helicopter pilot in Iraq, he got the GOP nomination to take on three-term U.S. Senator Debbie Stabenow in 2018 for two reasons: No better-known Republican wanted it, and Donald Trump liked him.
The seat was seen as unwinnable, and Mr. James indeed lost. But he lost by less than seven points; running far ahead of other Republicans on the statewide ballot. Six years before, a well-known and well-funded congressman had lost to her by more than 20 points.
Two years later, in 2020, Mr. James took on U.S. Sen. Gary Peters. He lost again, but this time by less than 2 percent, and ran ahead of President Trump. Two years later, Mr. James ran for a Macomb County seat in Congress he was expected to automatically win. Democrats ran an elderly retired judge who had little funding. To both parties’ shock, Mr. James, who spent millions, very nearly lost, winning by less than half a percentage point.
He did a little better when he was re-elected two years ago, but when he announced he was running for governor, Donald Trump told him not to do that and to stay in the House instead.
Mike Rogers, a former congressman who is running unopposed for the Republican nomination for the U.S. Senate, also told Mr. James not to run. The reason why was clear: Republicans feel their chances of holding on to the House are both more important and more likely than keeping Michigan’s statehouse.
Mr. James, who is now 45, responded by not saying yes or no, but essentially disappearing from public view, and making few public appearances and dodging debates with the three other GOP candidates who will be on the primary ballot.
At long last, Trump endorsed him Monday. Even before that, he was leading his two main opponents, businessman Perry Johnson and former Michigan Attorney General Mike Cox, who lost a bid for the nomination in 2010. A third opponent, Michigan Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt, ran commercials in which he is seen castrating hogs, saying that proves he can handle difficult jobs.
That didn’t get him far, and Monday he dropped out. Mr. Johnson, who is 78, has raised a stir by spending millions on ads claiming Michigan can do without an income tax, and says he intends to abolish the FBI, though it doesn’t seem likely a governor could do that.
He also ran four years ago, but was thrown off the ballot when it turned out most of his petition signatures were fraudulent; people he’d hired went to jail. Mr. Johnson, a world champion bridge player, next spent millions running for president, but ended his campaign after failing to attract measureable support.
The primary election race on the Democratic side would seem very one-sided, with Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson far ahead of her only opponent, Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson.
But Mr. Swanson has vowed to “not let the race be a coronation,” and recently was endorsed by the Teamsters’ union.
Coming next week: A look at the Democratic race for governor, and a possible major conflict of interest.
Mr. Lessenberry is a former national editor for The Blade. Contact him at: omblade@aol.com.
